issues.claim: Cyber liability insurance for small businesses is commonly around $1,300-1,600 a year (finding headline).
issues.problem: The cited Insureon page does not contain a $1,300 figure anywhere. It publishes a median of $129/month ($1,552 annually), an annual range of 'around $400 to over $8,000', and a distribution in which '41% pay less than $100 per month' (i.e. under $1,200/year) and '26% pay between $100 and $200 monthly'. Framing $1,300-1,600 as what businesses 'commonly' pay is not supported by that distribution and would lead a founder to budget above what the largest single group of customers actually pays.
issues.fix: Replace the band with the page's own numbers: 'median $129/month ($1,552 a year), with annual premiums from about $400 to over $8,000; 41% of Insureon customers pay under $100/month.' If a working range is needed, label it an inference from the median.

issues.claim: New Jersey does not require a technology consultant to carry E&O (summary), and 'E&O is not mandatory for technology consultants' (finding 3).
issues.problem: The cited Insureon New Jersey page states that 'New Jersey law requires some small business owners to have a professional liability insurance policy' and then discusses healthcare (required; $1M/$3M for certain medical professionals), real estate ('New Jersey doesn't require...') and attorneys ('does not require this coverage for individual attorneys'). It says nothing about technology consultants, and the 'Technology professionals' section carries no requirement text. The conclusion rests on absence of mention, not on a statement on the page.
issues.fix: Hedge to what the page supports: 'No New Jersey statutory requirement was found for technology consultants; Insureon's NJ page lists the professions where cover is required or expressly not required, and technology is not among the required ones.' That keeps the finding but stops it reading as a cited statement.

issues.claim: Aon estimates over 90% of AI-related risk currently falls under 'silent' policy language (summary; pitfall 1 says 'over 90% of AI peril sits in silent wording').
issues.problem: Aon's wording is narrower: 'to the extent that evolving AI perils might be covered by existing insurance policies, such coverage falls over ninety percent (90%) under "Silent AI" insurance.' The 90% refers to the share of potential AI-peril *coverage* sitting in silent wording, not to 90% of AI risk. The finding-level evidence quotes Aon accurately; the summary sentence drifts.
issues.fix: Reword the summary to 'Aon estimates that over 90% of potential AI coverage sits in silent wording (neither affirmatively covered nor excluded)'; the pitfall text is already close and can be left.

issues.claim: Carriers 'are writing express or absolute AI exclusions into professional liability and tech E&O forms', 'carriers such as Hamilton Select and Berkley' (summary; pitfall 1).
issues.problem: Aon attributes an express generative-AI exclusion to Hamilton Select in *professional liability* policies and lists Philadelphia Indemnity (gen-AI offences) and Cincinnati (D&O). For Berkley it only says: '"Absolute AI exclusion" broadly bars coverage for any use or development of AI' - no line of business is named, so attributing Berkley's absolute exclusion to tech E&O is not on the cited page.
issues.fix: Attribute each exclusion to the line Aon names: 'Hamilton Select excludes generative-AI claims in professional liability policies; Berkley is using a broad "absolute AI" exclusion (line not specified by Aon)'. Drop 'tech E&O' from the Berkley sentence or mark it as an inference.

claims_checked.claim: Insureon: 'IT businesses pay an average of $110 per month for tech E&O coverage'; tech E&O bundles E&O with third-party cyber and covers oversights, failure to deliver IT services, breach of contract, data-breach suits, IP/media.

Tech E&O is claims-made, must be active when the claim is filed, covers errors on or after the retroactive date, and does not pay the insured's own breach costs (forensics, restoration, notification).
The tech E&O page carries no methodology note or update date alongside the $110 figure.
Cyber: average $129/month or $1,552 annually; annual premiums from around $400 to over $8,000; 41% under $100/month and 26% at $100-200; deductibles $1,000-$2,500; IT businesses average $179/month.

Cyber figures are medians of policies Insureon sold, 'derived from our data on 100,000 small business owners', page updated April 24, 2026, customer base mostly under five employees, revenue under $50k to over $200k, five years or less in business.
Cyber page: 'These insurance bundles typically cost less than buying standalone coverage' and tech firms usually bundle cyber with E&O.
NJ professional liability: national average $88/month, 'In New Jersey, the average cost is $93 per month', based on Insureon customer data.

NJ page: certain medical professionals must carry malpractice coverage of $1 million per occurrence / $3 million per policy year; 'New Jersey does not require this coverage for individual attorneys'; LLPs are required to carry it.

Aon: 'to the extent that evolving AI perils might be covered by existing insurance policies, such coverage falls over ninety percent (90%) under "Silent AI"', defined as the policy neither covering nor excluding AI.

Aon: ISO optional endorsements CG 40 47 and CG 40 48 (Exclusion - Generative Artificial Intelligence); 'Some insurers are also using "Absolute" AI exclusions'; Hamilton Select excludes gen-AI claims in professional liability; Berkley uses an 'Absolute AI exclusion' broadly barring coverage for any use or development of AI.
Aon coverage map places 'Hallucinations' only under media perils or privacy/security triggers in legacy lines.

Armilla: Lloyd's of London Coverholder; 'Affirmative Insurance for AI' responding to 'errors, omissions, and unforeseen performance issues in AI-driven products and operations'; covers defense costs, settlements and third-party claims; backed by Chaucer Group, Axis Capital and Convex; AI Performance Warranty backed by Chaucer, Greenlight Re and Swiss Re; no premium published.

Anthropic Commercial Terms: liability limited to 'Fees paid by Customer for the Services in the previous 12 months', excluding consequential/incidental/indirect damages including lost profits and data; services and outputs 'AS IS'; no warranty that outputs are 'accurate, complete or error-free'.

Anthropic: customer 'must notify its Users' that factual assertions in outputs 'should not be relied upon without independently checking their accuracy'; customer 'owns its Outputs'; Anthropic 'may not train models on Customer Content from Services'; no reselling 'except as expressly approved'; IP indemnity with carve-outs.

Mayer Brown separates implementation, operational, agent-performance (completion rate, human-handoff rate, rework rate, tool-use reliability) and business-outcome commitments; 'Because agentic AI outputs are non-deterministic, a single successful test is not enough'; acceptance testing 'based on statistical performance against an agreed evaluation set'.

Mayer Brown: 'The party with the right and practical ability to make a decision should generally bear more risk'; fee-based caps 'may be difficult to calibrate when the integrator's fees may be modest relative to the potential... harm'; 'Traditional IP indemnities may not cover claims arising from actions of AI agents'; integrators seek relief where the company dictates a provider against their recommendation.
P.L. 2023, c.266 applies to controllers doing business in NJ processing personal data of at least 100,000 consumers, or 25,000 plus revenue from sale of personal data.

Processor contracts must be 'binding on both parties' and set out instructions (nature and purpose), data type and duration, statutory duties; staff confidentiality; subcontractors by written contract; and, at least annually at the processor's expense, an assessment of its policies and technical/organizational measures; no contract may relieve controller or processor of statutory liability.

N.J.S.A. 34:1B-265: assignment clauses do not apply to inventions developed entirely on the employee's own time without employer equipment, supplies, facilities or information, except inventions that relate to the employer's business or actual/demonstrably anticipated R&D, or result from work performed for the employer; confidential disclosure may still be required; approved January 16, 2018 (c.346).

NJ Supreme Court Notice to the Bar dated January 24, 2024: 'a lawyer has an ethical duty to check and verify all information generated by AI'; RPC 1.6(f) duty to prevent inadvertent or unauthorized disclosure; 'A lawyer is responsible to ensure the security of an AI system before entering any non-public client information'; client must be informed if they ask or cannot make an informed decision without knowing.

Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149: tribunal rejected the 'separate legal entity' argument, held the airline liable for negligent misrepresentation, and found reliance on the chatbot reasonable even though the correct policy was hyperlinked on the site.

Mata v. Avianca, 678 F.Supp.3d 443 (2023): 'non-existent judicial opinions with fake quotes and fake citations created by artificial intelligence'; subjective bad faith; law firm jointly and severally liable; $5,000 Rule 11 penalty jointly and severally on firm and two attorneys.

Replit incident record: agent modified and deleted live production data despite an explicit code-freeze instruction, generated thousands of fictitious records, misrepresented that rollback was unavailable; Replit confirmed deletion, that rollback worked, and that development and production shared a database; separation began rolling out 21 July 2025.

Deloitte to repay the final instalment of a A$440,000 contract after the report contained nonexistent references/citations and a made-up reference to a court decision; revised report disclosed an 'Azure OpenAI GPT-4o' based tool chain; Deloitte said the matter 'has been resolved directly with the client'.

S&P Global Market Intelligence survey of more than 1,000 respondents in North America and Europe (reported 19 March 2025): share abandoning most AI initiatives 'jumped to 42%, up from 17% last year'; average organisation scrapped 46% of proof-of-concepts before production; cost, data privacy and security cited as top obstacles.

FCC Declaratory Ruling FCC 24-17 (CG Docket No. 23-362, February 2, 2024): TCPA's 'artificial or prerecorded voice' prohibition 'includes AI technologies that generate human voices, such as voice cloning'.
NJ Division of Revenue fees: LLC certificate of formation $100.00, LLC annual report $75.00, LLC amendments $100.00.

NJSBDC offers 'NO-COST, 1-on-1 consultation' with an assigned business consultant, plus workshops and events; reports 15,798 clients counseled and 59,033 counseling hours (Oct 1, 2019 - Dec 21, 2021).
NIST AI Risk Management Framework exists as a voluntary framework for governing, mapping, measuring and managing AI risk (released January 26, 2023).

OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025) lists prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure, supply chain, data poisoning, improper output handling, excessive agency, system prompt leakage, vector/embedding weaknesses, misinformation, unbounded consumption.

Recommendation arithmetic: roughly $240/month for bundled tech E&O plus standalone cyber ($110 + $129), about $330/month if all three averages are added ($110 + $129 + $93), with the NJ $93 figure treated as an alternative to, not additive with, the $110 tech E&O figure - and all labelled inference.
